overview: Oceania Healthcare is a New Zealand-listed operator of retirement villages and aged care centres, accommodating approximately 3,900 residents (around 2,200 care residents) across sites from Northland to the South Island. The business runs a dual-segment model: it sells Occupation Right Agreements (ORAs) across its independent living units (ILUs) and premium care suites, while earning recurring income from government-funded and premium-pay residential aged care. Under CEO Suzanne Dvorak (appointed July 2024) and Chair Elizabeth (Liz) Coutts, Oceania completed FY2026 (year ended 31 March 2026, results announced 22 May 2026) as a 'record' year on its operating metrics: total assets reached $3.1bn, Proforma Underlying EBITDA rose 20% to $97.7m (statutory Underlying EBITDA $97.4m, +13%), record ORA receipts of $336.2m, 603 units sold (+16%), and net debt cut by $121m to $507m (gearing 30.1%, the low end of the 30-35% target). Reported NPAT fell to just $0.1m, but this reflects a smaller non-cash fair value gain on investment property, not operating deterioration. FY2026 was the foundation-building close-out ahead of the FY27-FY31 'Path to FY31' growth phase.

business_model.summary: Oceania operates the Occupation Right Agreement (ORA) model standard to NZ retirement villages, combined with a differentiated 'care premiumisation' strategy. Residents pay a lump-sum ORA price for the right to occupy an independent living unit or care suite; on departure, Oceania retains a Deferred Management Fee (DMF) of roughly 25-30% and resells (replenishes) the ORA. This creates a capital-recycling engine in which ORA receipts (a record $336.2m in FY26) fund debt repayment and development. The care segment earns government-subsidised fees for standard care beds and charges Premium Accommodation Charges (PACs) and care suite DMFs for higher-acuity premium care. New development generates one-time development margins (care suite development margin ran at 40% in FY26 on new sales). The strategic emphasis is shifting mix toward private-pay care suites, lifting Underlying EBITDA per occupied bed.
business_model.customer_type: B2C - predominantly residents 75+ seeking independent retirement living or residential aged care. Mix of government-subsidised (means-tested) and privately-funded ('self-pay') residents. Oceania targets the premium segment, particularly through its care suite product and The Helier luxury offering in Auckland.
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand only. Portfolio concentrated in Auckland (key development/flagship sites: The Helier, Meadowbank, Franklin, Lady Allum) plus major regional centres (Hamilton, Tauranga, Christchurch, Hawke's Bay, Nelson/Blenheim, Northland). FY26 reshaped the portfolio toward larger integrated villages, divesting seven smaller sites.
business_model.key_cash_flows: ORA receipts are the primary cash-generation driver - FY26 receipts from new ORAs were a record $336.2m (vs $294.5m FY25, +14%), the largest lever to repay development debt. Operating cash flow rose sharply (the DCF model cites FY26 OCF of $169.4m, +54%, helped by record ORA receipts). Reported Free Cash Flow from Operations (after development capex) was a $(15.0)m outflow ex one-offs, a 64% improvement on FY25's $(41.7)m; management targets positive operating FCF in FY27, which is the trigger to resume dividends.

revenue_streams.name: Care Operations (beds & care suites)
revenue_streams.notes: FY26 care revenue ~$208.6m (the bulk of operating revenue). Includes government-funded beds, PAC fees and care suite DMF accrual. Care premiumisation is the key driver: Underlying EBITDA per occupied bed (incl. capital and resale gains) rose 40% to $27.2k in FY26 (from $19.4k FY25); excluding capital gains it rose 43%. More than half the portfolio now generates well above prior levels, driven by sell-down of care suite stock at The Helier, Redwood, Meadowbank and Ōrākei.

revenue_streams.name: Village Operations (ILU weekly fees & DMF accrual)
revenue_streams.notes: Weekly service fees plus accrued DMF over the occupancy period. Supported in FY26 by record ILU/villa sales (Franklin Stage 1 villas, Meadowbank, The Helier ILUs reaching 74% sell-down).

revenue_streams.name: Other / Corporate
revenue_streams.notes: Wesley Institute of Nursing Education closed April 2025; FY26 Proforma figures are adjusted for its removal. Corporate segment costs were broadly contained as the $20.4m cost-out programme delivered.

main_competitors: Ryman Healthcare (RYM.NZ) - largest NZ operator, NZ and Australia
Summerset Group (SUM.NZ) - second largest NZ operator, strong development pipeline and customer satisfaction
Arvida Group - merged with Bupa NZ retirement villages; large NZ operator (taken private/under offer in recent years)
Bupa New Zealand - large private care-home operator (UK-listed parent)
competitive_position.market_position: Third or fourth largest NZ retirement village operator by unit count, differentiated by an integrated care-retirement model and premium care suite innovation. Smaller than Ryman and Summerset but larger than most private operators. FY26 strategy deliberately reshaped the portfolio toward larger integrated villages while divesting seven smaller, lower-return sites.

moat_factors.description: Oceania pioneered the care suite model in NZ (premium private-pay care accommodation under an ORA structure), generating higher per-bed revenue and shifting exposure from government funding to private-pay. FY26 care suite development margin was 40% and Underlying EBITDA per occupied bed jumped 40% to $27.2k, evidencing the structural margin uplift from this strategy.

A combined retirement-living and aged-care offering under one roof creates stickiness - residents can age in place from independent living through dementia care without relocating. The nurse-practitioner-led model and in-house primary care (being brought in-house) reinforce clinical differentiation and resident retention.

A development pipeline of roughly 1,270 gross units (per the DCF model), including the Franklin greenfield (Stage 1's 31 villas delivered Jan 2026 at ~80% sell-down, with further expansion land) and The Helier Stage 2 expansion land. Provides optionality for 100-150 units/yr development once gearing is reduced - which FY26's deleveraging now enables.

Care-centre certification from Te Whatu Ora (Health NZ) creates regulatory barriers to entry. Established licences, sites and resident relationships are difficult and slow for new entrants to replicate.

moat_factors.factor: Capital-recycling ORA float and asset backing
moat_factors.description: The ORA model provides a large, low-cost, recycling 'float' of resident loans. Combined with a property-heavy balance sheet (>90% of $3.08bn total assets are property at fair value), it underpins NTA per share of $1.62 - well above the $0.76 share price - providing asset-backed downside support, though realisation is gradual.

business.risk: Unsold development stock overhang (esp. The Helier)
business.description: Material unsold development stock remains, with care suites alone representing ~$69.3m (54% currently occupied by non-ORA/PAC residents). The Helier ILUs reached 74% sell-down/under application and care residences 53% occupied/under application as at 20 May 2026 - much improved and nearing development cost recovery, but slower-than-original-plan sell-through of premium stock still risks delaying debt reduction and questions the depth of NZ's ultra-premium retirement market.

ORA prices and resale/development margins are correlated with NZ house prices, and purchasers typically fund ORA entry from home-sale proceeds. FY26 was delivered against a 'subdued residential property market', and margins moderated as Oceania cycled out of higher-margin legacy stock. A sustained downturn would suppress demand, slow resales and compress margins.

business.risk: Execution of the FY27-FY31 growth phase
business.description: Oceania must pivot from balance-sheet repair to disciplined development growth (toward 100-150 units/yr) without re-leveraging. Premature acceleration of development, or greenfield delivery risk (Franklin's multi-stage broadacre build), could jeopardise the hard-won gearing improvement. Significant recent leadership change adds transformation risk.
Ryman and Summerset are larger, well-capitalised competitors with stronger brands and development pipelines, creating pricing and share pressure, particularly in premium Auckland sub-markets.

financial.description: Despite cutting net debt $121m to $507m (gearing 30.1%, low end of target) in FY26, the balance sheet still carries ~$517m total debt. A mix of variable-rate bank facilities and fixed-rate retail bonds creates refinancing risk on bond maturities at potentially higher rates, and any sales slowdown would slow further deleveraging. ICR remains comfortably above the 2.0x covenant after lower drawn debt and OCR cuts.

financial.risk: Reported earnings volatility from property fair value
financial.description: Reported NPAT collapsed to $0.1m in FY26 (from $30.4m) purely because the non-cash fair value gain on investment property fell to $32.8m (from $90.2m), compounded by Holidays Act remediation and restructure costs. This makes statutory EPS and P/E uninformative; investors must use Underlying EBITDA, Underlying NPAT ($63.7m, Proforma $64.1m), embedded value and NTA instead - a recurring source of investor confusion and share-price discount.

financial.risk: Deep discount to NTA / equity-raising constraint
financial.description: NTA per share rose to $1.62 (from $1.51) yet the shares trade at $0.76 - a ~53% discount. The market discounts the carrying value of property and/or expects sustained underperformance versus NTA. The discount limits the ability to raise equity accretively and is the central valuation tension.
NZD-only operations; no material currency risk.

regulatory.description: The NZ Government's review of the Retirement Villages Act 2003 contemplates measures such as mandatory buyback periods (paying departing residents/families while awaiting ORA resale), greater transparency and stronger dispute resolution. A mandatory buyback requirement would increase working-capital needs and reduce the capital efficiency of the ORA model for all operators. Oceania manages buyback obligations within its capital priorities and continues to monitor the reform closely; timing and final form remain uncertain.

regulatory.risk: Health NZ certification and care quality standards
regulatory.description: Care operations require certification from Te Whatu Ora (Health NZ). Tightening quality standards and staffing ratios raise compliance costs, and non-compliance can remove certification and materially impair care revenue. Oceania invests in its clinical/nurse-practitioner model to maintain compliance.

An Aged Care review/advisory process is underway (the Board explicitly noted it looks forward to its recommendations). Changes to means-testing, self-pay contributions or the funding model could shift the mix between government-subsidised and private-pay residents and affect care revenue. Government funding has historically lagged cost inflation, a risk Oceania mitigates by pivoting toward private-pay care suites.

macro.description: ORA resale gains and development margins depend on underlying property values. FY26 was delivered against a subdued market; a weak or stalling property cycle would slow ORA velocity, depress pricing and compress development margins - the single largest external swing factor for cash generation.

Both direct (variable-rate bank debt) and indirect (property market and ORA affordability). Falling RBNZ OCR through 2025-26 has been a tailwind, lowering interest costs and supporting house prices; a reversal would raise financing costs and dampen ORA demand.

macro.risk: NZ economic conditions and consumer confidence
macro.description: New residents often fund ORA entry from home sales, so soft consumer confidence and a weak economy slow decision-making and sales cadence even where underlying care demand is non-discretionary.

Aged care is labour-intensive; wage inflation and periodic nursing shortages pressure margins. FY26 included a Holidays Act remediation charge. Bringing primary care in-house adds clinical capability but also staffing dependency. Structural long-term nursing shortage risk persists as care demand grows.

growth_drivers: Demographic tailwind: NZ's 75+ population is projected to roughly double by ~2050, with a structural shortage of residential care beds, underpinning long-run, largely non-discretionary demand for Oceania's integrated care-village model. The Board describes demand for quality retirement living and aged care as strong and growing.

Care premiumisation inflection: Underlying EBITDA per occupied bed rose 40% to $27.2k in FY26 (43% ex capital gains), driven by selling down care suite stock and shifting mix from government-funded beds to private-pay care suites. Continued migration of the portfolio toward this higher per-bed economics is the core margin driver.
Cost-out programme: The ~$20.4m annualised savings programme delivered in FY26 ($13.2m in-year), with full run-rate benefit landing in FY27, providing operating leverage on top of revenue growth.

Deleveraging unlocks development: Net debt cut $121m to $507m and gearing to 30.1% (low end of target) creates the balance-sheet headroom to restart development toward 100-150 units/yr from FY27-28, including Franklin expansion and The Helier Stage 2, at attractive care-suite development margins (~40% in FY26).

Record sales cadence: 603 units sold (+16%) and record ORA receipts of $336.2m demonstrate restored sales momentum; Franklin Stage 1 at ~80% sell-down and The Helier ILUs at 74% are ahead of expectations.

Capital recycling via divestments: Seven smaller sites divested in FY26 for $51.1m released capital at or near carrying value to reduce debt and concentrate the portfolio on larger integrated villages.

Dividend resumption optionality: A 40-60% of Free Cash Flow from Operations policy is in place; resumption (expected once operating FCF turns positive, targeted FY27) should broaden the income-investor buyer base and support a re-rating toward NTA.
Falling RBNZ OCR: Lower rates reduce financing costs on variable bank debt and support the NZ property market and ORA affordability.

recent_developments.event: FY2026 full-year results (year ended 31 March 2026): record year on operating metrics. Revenue $267.1m (+3%); statutory Underlying EBITDA $97.4m (+13%), Proforma Underlying EBITDA $97.7m (+20%); Underlying NPAT $63.7m (Proforma $64.1m, +34% on pcp); reported NPAT $0.1m (down from $30.4m, driven by a smaller non-cash fair value gain of $32.8m vs $90.2m). Total assets reached $3.1bn; NTA per share $1.62 (from $1.51). Record ORA receipts $336.2m (+14%); 603 units sold (+16%). No final dividend declared.

Balance sheet repair completed: net debt reduced by $121m to $507m and gearing cut to 30.1% (from 36.3%), at the low end of the 30-35% target range. Achieved via record ORA receipts and $51.1m of divestment proceeds. CEO/executive incentive targets for both Underlying EBITDA and net debt reduction were met (150% stretch on the net debt KPI).

Care premiumisation milestone: Underlying EBITDA per occupied bed (incl. capital and resale gains) rose 40% to $27.2k (from $19.4k FY25); excluding capital gains +43%. Care suite development margin on new sales was 40%, driven by sales at The Helier, Redwood, Meadowbank and Ōrākei.

The Helier (Auckland flagship) ILU sell-down/under-application reached 74% and care residences 53% occupied/under application (as at 20 May 2026), nearing development cost recovery. Franklin Stage 1 (31 villas, delivered January 2026) at ~80% sell-down, ahead of expectations; expansion land secured for further Franklin and The Helier Stage 2 stages.

Portfolio reshaping: seven smaller sites (including Ohinemuri, Whitianga, Woburn, Hutt Gables, Eldon and others) divested during FY26 for total proceeds of $51.1m, at or around carrying value, focusing the portfolio on larger integrated villages.
Franklin Village Stage 1 (31 villas plus community facilities) delivered to first residents, Oceania's first large greenfield broadacre development.

Investor Day: 'Path to FY31' strategy unveiled - FY26-FY27 foundation priorities (sell-down stock, cut debt, cut costs, lift care profitability) followed by an FY27-FY31 growth phase targeting disciplined, value-accretive development. ~$20.4m annualised cost-out target and a revised 40-60% of Free Cash Flow from Operations dividend policy confirmed.
Wesley Institute of Nursing Education closed; FY26 Proforma Underlying figures are adjusted to remove its prior-year contribution.
Suzanne Dvorak appointed CEO; subsequent executive renewal (new Chief Sales & Marketing Officer Nov 2024, elevated clinical leadership) drove the operational turnaround now evidenced in FY26 results.

bull_case: FY26 proves the turnaround is real and de-risks the thesis: record ORA receipts ($336.2m), 603 units sold, Proforma Underlying EBITDA +20%, and a $121m cut in net debt to gearing of 30.1% (low end of target) materially reduce the prior covenant/leverage risk and lift the floor under equity value.

Care premiumisation is a structural margin engine: Underlying EBITDA per occupied bed jumped 40% to $27.2k in one year, with 40% care-suite development margins. As the rest of the portfolio migrates toward these economics, care segment earnings can grow substantially without new development.

Deep discount to NTA provides asset-backed margin of safety: NTA per share of $1.62 versus a $0.76 share price (~53% discount) on a property-heavy ($3.1bn assets) balance sheet. Sustained FCF generation, debt reduction and dividend resumption could drive a re-rating toward NTA - the DCF's bull case implies intrinsic value of ~$1.60.

Cost-out plus operating leverage: full $20.4m cost-out run-rate from FY27, on top of revenue growth and a falling RBNZ OCR cutting interest costs, should lift Underlying NPAT and convert the operating recovery into positive Free Cash Flow from Operations.

Development optionality re-opens: with the balance sheet repaired, the ~1,270-unit pipeline (Franklin expansion, The Helier Stage 2, others) can restart toward 100-150 units/yr at attractive care-suite margins, reigniting development-margin growth into the FY27-FY31 phase.
Dividend resumption catalyst: a 40-60% of operating FCF policy, expected to trigger once FCF turns positive (targeted FY27), should broaden the NZX income-investor base and support the share price.
bear_case: Dividend remains suspended with no firm date: no final FY26 dividend, and resumption is gated on positive Free Cash Flow from Operations (still a $(15.0)m outflow ex one-offs in FY26). Income-focused NZX investors may keep avoiding the stock until cash dividends actually resume, weighing on the price versus dividend-paying peers like Summerset.

Property-market dependence: FY26's record sales came despite a subdued property market, and management flagged margins moderating as it cycled out of higher-margin stock. A sustained NZ housing downturn would slow ORA velocity, depress resale and development margins, and stall further deleveraging.

Premium-stock sell-through risk: The Helier care residences are still only 53% occupied/under application and unsold care suites of ~$69.3m remain. Slow absorption of premium stock would delay full cost recovery and debt reduction, and raises questions about NZ's depth of ultra-premium retirement demand.

Retirement Villages Act reform could impair ORA economics: proposed mandatory buyback requirements would lift working-capital needs and reduce the capital efficiency of the ORA model sector-wide; the timing and severity remain uncertain.

Reported earnings optics and NTA discount persist: statutory NPAT of just $0.1m (on a smaller fair-value gain) gives the headline a poor look, and the ~53% discount to $1.62 NTA has been durable - the market may continue to discount asset carrying values and constrain equity-funded growth until a multi-year track record of positive FCF and dividends is established.

Scale disadvantage: Ryman and Summerset's larger scale, brands and development pipelines give them durable cost, marketing and growth advantages, making it harder for the smaller Oceania to invest at the same rate.
